podcast.title: CBGB Founding Vision (December 1973)
podcast.body: Hilly Crystal, formerly the manager of The Village Vanguard, leased a former biker bar space in the Bowery, New York City, in December 1973. His original intent was for a venue featuring country, bluegrass, and blues music, which he named CBGB, adding OMFUG (Other Music For Uplifting Gourmandizers) to sound "uncouth or crude." "In December 1973, Hilly Crystal, the former manager of the village vanguard, he leased a space in the Bowery in New York City that was formerly a biker bar."

podcast.title: Founder of CBGB (1973)
podcast.body: Hilly Crystal, an ex-marine, opened the CBGB club in 1973 in the Bowery neighborhood of New York. Despite the area being an economic and social disaster zone at the time, the cheap rent allowed starving artists to live, rehearse, and create. Crystal established the club's musical policy, which fostered an environment where artists, "freaks, and weirdos" could do their own thing, leading to the birth of punk rock. "When an ex-marine named Hilly Crystal opened the place in 1973, it was in a part of town where nobody wanted to go."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Ongoing History Book of Lasts

podcast.title: Closure of CBGB (2006)
podcast.body: Hilly Crystal was forced to close CBGB due to escalating financial pressures. Monthly rent had risen from $19,000 to $35,000, and the club faced a $90,000 lawsuit from a local residence committee. Despite court cases and an attempt to declare the club a historical landmark, the ongoing gentrification of the neighborhood and rising costs made it impossible to continue. "In the end, rent went up to $35,000 a month and Hilly had no choice but to close the place down."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Ongoing History Book of Lasts

podcast.title: Enduring Vision and Death (2007)
podcast.body: Crystal maintained his vision for CBGB as a venue for original music even as the punk scene evolved to feature "faster and angrier" bands like Murphy's Law and Bad Brains in the early 1980s. Despite legal battles and gentrification leading to the club's closure on October 15, 2006, Crystal died a year later in 2007. "Billy Crystal was not thrilled with all of it, but he kept true to his vision of CBGB being a venue for original music."

podcast.title: Early CBGB Environment
podcast.body: CBGB's location in a "pretty awful" Bowery neighborhood, below a flop house inhabited by alcoholics and Vietnam veterans, contributed to cheap rent and a lack of complaints about loud music. Despite the unsanitary conditions, including dodging liquor bottles and dog poop, Crystal fostered a unique musical environment. "It was nothing to have to step over the bodies of guys who were passed out on the sidewalks. Of course, this all meant that rent was cheap and nobody was really going to complain about loud music."

podcast.title: Original Music Rule
podcast.body: Crystal established a strict rule that all bands booked at his club must play only original music, stating, "originality to me was prime technique took second place." This principle guided CBGB's booking policies, even for bands he initially found unappealing. "Crystal had a very firm rule that any bands that were booked for his club could only play original music. He said originality to me was prime technique took second place."

srcs.episode: Ep. 57 - Punk and New Wave at New York's CBGB

podcast.title: Patti Smith's Magnetism
podcast.body: Crystal was deeply impressed by Patti Smith's stage presence, observing that "she just had magnetism." He praised her vocal abilities, noting that she "stayed on pitch, she bent the notes just right, she sang real well, she communicated," making her one of the few performers he could listen to repeatedly. "He said she just had magnetism. She may not have been a singer but she sure sounded like one."

srcs.episode: Ep. 57 - Punk and New Wave at New York's CBGB

podcast.title: Ramones' Loudness and Self-Reliance
podcast.body: Crystal's first impression of The Ramones was that they were "a very, very loud band" from Queens whom "nobody liked." He valued them because they consistently brought their own amplifiers and PA system, which CBGB could not afford. He recognized their hard work, self-belief, and their determination to "make themselves happen." "my first impression of the Ramones was that they were just a very, very loud band They'd come in from Queens where nobody liked them They worked very, very hard and played more and more."

srcs.episode: Ep. 57 - Punk and New Wave at New York's CBGB

podcast.title: Skepticism Towards Television
podcast.body: Crystal initially found Tom Verlaine's band, Television, to be "god awful" and "horrible" when they first started playing at CBGB, noting that their manager, Terry Ork, had to badger him repeatedly to book them. Despite his initial skepticism, their ability to draw an audience ensured their continued presence. "He kept saying, well, we'll have another band with them next time and we'll try some new things. It was always one thing or another thing to get them back."

xref.title: Pioneering Performances at CBGB (1973)
xref.body: In December 1973, band members Richard Hell, Richard Lloyd, and Tom Verlaine approached Hilly Crystal, owner of a bar named CBGBOMFUG, and secured a Sunday night slot for their band, Television, to perform for an admission fee of $1. After a challenging beginning, their performances at CBGB, combined with the earlier collapse of the Mercer Art Center, helped establish the club as the epicenter for New York's burgeoning punk rock scene. "Marina Half Weeks later, television played their first ever rock night at CBGB. And admission was $1."

xref.title: CBGB Debut (March 31, 1974)
xref.body: Tom Verlaine and Richard Hell approached Hilly Crystal in March 1974 about playing at CBGB. Hilly, believing they were into country, bluegrass, or blues, offered them Sunday nights for a $1 cover. Television played their first gig on March 31, 1974, marking the beginning of CBGB's "real era" as a rock venue. "Still, on March 31, 1974, television played their first gig, and their real era of CBGB had begun."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: CBGB Residency and Scene Growth
xref.body: Television's Sunday night residency quickly became one of the best nights at CBGB, drawing the crowd that had been displaced by the collapse of the Mercer Arts Center. This growing interest led Hilly Crystal to institute a rock-only policy within a few months of Television's debut, signifying the club's transformation into a hub for the new scene. "That Sunday night residency became one of the best nights of the week for CBGB, the crowd that had been displaced by the collapse of the Mercer Arts Center reconvened there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Disdain for CBGB
xref.body: The Ramones themselves didn't think highly of CBGB initially, finding the stage too small, Hilly Crystal unhygienic, and the club plagued by rats and mice. They also found the clientele unpleasant, noting patrons would relieve themselves in corners due to the awful bathrooms. "Now to be fair, the Ramones didn't think too much of CBGB either. This stage was too small. They thought Hilly needed to bathe more and they hated how his dog, all the rats and all the mice, cracked all over the place."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Residency at CBGB
xref.body: Television began playing a regular Sunday Night Residency at Hilly Crystal's bar, which would soon become widely known as CBGB. Their performances, starting around the same time that displaced artists from the Mercer Art Center began migrating to CBGB, helped establish the club as a hub for new music in New York City. "By the summer of 1974, Hilly's bar, now known just as CBGB to everyone, was hosting not just television, but the Ramones, Patty Smith, Suicide, Blondie, Talking Heads, the Heartbreakers, and a bunch of other groups."
